t.1.179.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the kings had desisted from the task of stringing the bow, then the noble-minded Jiṣṇu rose up from the midst of the brahmins.
t.1.179.2: The foremost of the brahmins shouted aloud, waving their deerskins, when they saw Pārtha setting forth, radiant as Indra's banner.
t.1.179.3: Some were downcast, some were filled with joy, and some, shrewd men who lived by their wits, spoke to one another.
t.1.179.4: That bow which the world-renowned kings headed by Karṇa and Śalya, mighty men devoted to the science of archery, could not bend.
t.1.179.6: The brāhmaṇas will become a laughingstock among all the kings if this deed, undertaken rashly and without due consideration, is not accomplished.
t.1.179.5: How then, O brahmins, can that bow be strung by a mere brahmin lad, unskilled in weapons and far weaker in strength?
t.1.179.7: If this man has set out to draw the bow out of pride, out of insolence, or out of a brahmin's rashness, let him be stopped; it is well that he should not go.
t.1.179.8: We shall not become a laughingstock, nor shall we have given ourselves over to frivolity, nor shall we incur the hatred of the kings in the world.
t.1.179.10: This feat may well be expected of him, and it is inferred from his zeal; his strength is joined with great zeal, for one without strength would not go forward of his own accord.
t.1.179.9: Some said, "This splendid youth is like the trunk of a king of elephants; with brawny shoulders, thighs and arms, he is like the Himālaya in steadfastness."
t.1.179.12: Living on water, living on air, eating only fruit, firm in their vows, the brahmins, though weak in body, are indeed the stronger by the fiery power of the brahman.
t.1.179.11: There is no deed whatsoever in the three worlds, among all beings that stand still and move, that would be impossible for brahmins.
t.1.179.13: A brāhmaṇa is not to be despised, whether he does what is good or what is bad, whatever deed has fallen to him, be it pleasant or painful, great or small.
t.1.179.15: Approaching that bow, he then circled it keeping it to his right; and, bowing his head to it, the scorcher of foes joyfully took it up.
t.1.179.14: While the brahmins were thus lamenting in various words, Arjuna stood near the bow, unmoving like a mountain.
t.1.179.17: Then a sound arose in the sky, and a great clamor arose in the midst of the assembly; the god rained down heavenly flowers upon the head of Pārtha, the slayer of his foes.
t.1.179.16: In the twinkling of an eye he strung the bow and took up arrows numbering half of ten. He pierced the target, and, pierced through, it suddenly fell through the opening to the ground.
t.1.179.18: Then on every side they waved their garments and raised loud cries, and showers of flowers fell there from the sky all around.
t.1.179.20: Seeing him, Drupada, the slayer of foes, was pleased, and he, together with his army, wished to come to the aid of Pārtha.
t.1.179.19: The musicians played instruments of a hundred parts, and throngs of sūtas and māgadhas, sweet-voiced, sang praises there.
t.1.179.22: Seeing the target pierced, and beholding Pārtha, who was like Śakra, Kṛṣṇā took up a splendid garland of white flowers and, smiling, went to the son of Kuntī.
t.1.179.21: But when that great uproar had arisen, Yudhiṣṭhira, the foremost of those who uphold dharma, went swiftly back to their dwelling together with the twins, those best of men.
t.1.179.23: Having won her in the arena and taken her with him, he of inconceivable deeds, honored by those twice-born men, went forth from the arena, followed by her, his wife.
